content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe how electrons are arranged in shells
State the maximum number of electrons in each shell
Write electron configurations for the first 20 elements
Relate electron configuration to position in the Periodic Table
Electrons are not randomly scattered around the nucleus - they are arranged in specific
(also called energy levels). Understanding electron arrangement is crucial because it determines how atoms bond and react.
Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus. Each shell:
Can hold a maximum number of electrons
Fills from the innermost shell outwards
The nth shell can hold up to 2n² electrons.
Explore electronic configuration — arrange electrons into shells and subshells for different elements using the interactive visualisation below.
describes how electrons are distributed among the shells. It is written as a series of numbers separated by commas.
Electrons fill the lowest energy shell first (closest to nucleus)
Each shell must be full before the next shell starts filling
For elements 1-20, electrons fill shells 1, 2, 3, then 4
Mark electrons as dots or crosses
Show nucleus in centre with atomic number
Fill inner shells completely before outer shells
Electron configuration is directly related to position in the Periodic Table:
Electrons in outer shell = Group number
Group 0/8: 8 electrons in outer shell (full outer shell)
Write the electron configuration for sulfur (atomic number 16).
An atom has the electron configuration 2, 8, 3. Identify the element and its position in the Periodic Table.
Writing 2, 8, 9 for potassium (putting 9 in third shell)
The third shell holds 8 for elements 1-20; potassium is 2, 8, 8, 1
Adding more than 2 electrons to the first shell
The first shell can only hold 2 electrons maximum
Forgetting that electrons = protons in a neutral atom
Always check: total electrons = atomic number
Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus
Shells fill from the inside out: 2, 8, 8, then 2 for elements 1-20
Electron configuration is written as numbers separated by commas (e.g., 2, 8, 1)
Electrons in outer shell = Group number
Elements in the same group have similar chemical properties because they have the same number of outer electrons
